newsitem.title: USA: Democrats, Republicans find some common goals.
newsitem.headline: Democrats, Republicans find some common goals.

text.p: The U.S. Senate's Republican and Democratic leaders on Tuesday unveiled rival agendas for the coming year with many common themes -- lower taxes, a balanced budget, anti-crime efforts and aid for education.

With only a glance toward the ethics fray dominating their counterparts on the other side of the Capitol, the Senate leaders said they hoped their renewed bipartisan spirit would help push them toward legislative compromises.

"We differ on strategies, not goals. I'm hopeful we can find ways to achieve our goals that are acceptable to both parties," Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle of South Dakota said as he introduced his party's 12 legislative priorities.
Senate Republican Whip Don Nickles sounded a similar note at his news conference, saying, "This is a chance for this Congress to work together with the Democrats to enact legislation."

The standout of the Republicans' 11-point package was a $170 billion tax cut over the next five years with a $500 per child tax credit, a capital gains tax cut, reduced estate taxes and expanded retirement accounts.

On the House side where tax bills must begin, Ways and Means Committee chairman Bill Archer applauded the plan but expressed reservations about how large the tax cut could be. "The more tax relief we can give to hard-hit working Americans the better off we are going to be as a country," he said, but added that he would not act until he knew "how much room there is in there (the budget) for tax relief."

Daschle said the Republican tax cut was too large. Democrats will take their tax cut cue from President Bill Clinton, who is expected to unveil a smaller package of tax reductions with his budget on Feb. 6. But his Democrats proposed a way for investors in small businesses to reinvest gains without paying tax, expanded retirement accounts and help for farmers.
The White House has said it will wage a determined campaign against the Republicans' number one item, a constitutional amendment to require a balanced budget.

Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott of Mississippi said the vote may be held by the end of February but Republican sources said they had not underestimated the difficulty of rounding up the 12 Democrats necessary to win.
The balanced budget proposal failed by one vote last year, needing 67 votes to pass. Republicans control the Senate 55-45.
